name: Cà Mau Cape
summary: The southern tip of mainland Vietnam, where mangrove forests grow out into the sea and the coastline keeps changing.

eras.label: Long ago
eras.title: Land from the river
eras.text: The whole peninsula is made of mud carried down by the Mekong and pushed along the coast by currents. Mangroves trap it among their roots and slowly turn it into land.

eras.label: 18th century
eras.title: On the sea charts
eras.text: European navigators sailing between India and China marked the cape on their charts, as on this anonymous Portuguese chart of the peninsula and the Mekong.

image.file: Carte marine anonyme portugaise de la péninsule de Ca Mau et du delta du Mékong - btv1b532875781 (1 of 2).jpg
image.alt: A Portuguese sea chart of the Cà Mau peninsula

eras.title: A national park
eras.text: Mũi Cà Mau National Park was created to protect the mangroves and mudflats at the tip of the peninsula.

image.file: Rhizophora apiculata in Dat Mui, Vietnam.jpg

eras.title: A biosphere reserve
eras.text: UNESCO named the area a Biosphere Reserve, and in 2013 it was listed as a Ramsar wetland of international importance.

image.file: A wooden fence in mudflats in Dat Mui.jpg

eras.label: Today
eras.title: The end of the land
eras.text: A monument in the shape of a ship's prow and a marker of the national coordinates stand at the tip, facing the sea.

image.alt: The monument at Cà Mau Cape

story.title: Land that moves
story.narration: Cà Mau's coastline is never still. On some shores, mud settles among the mangrove roots and the land creeps out into the sea year after year. On others, waves and rising seas wear the coast away, and whole rows of trees fall into the water. Local people plant mangroves and build bamboo fences in the mud to hold the land. At the cape, standing on ground that did not exist a few generations ago, you can see the Mekong Delta being made.

story.title: The prince of Bạc Liêu
story.narration: In the early 20th century, Trần Trinh Huy, the son of a hugely rich landowner in Bạc Liêu, became famous as the 'Bạc Liêu prince' for his extravagance. Stories about him are told all over the south. In the best known, a woman at a party dropped something in the dark, and he lit a banknote to help her search for it. Many of these tales are exaggerated, but his family's grand house still stands in Bạc Liêu.

story.title: A song of longing
story.narration: In 1919, the Bạc Liêu musician Cao Văn Lầu wrote 'Dạ cổ hoài lang', 'Hearing the night drum, missing my husband'. It tells of a wife waiting for a husband who has gone far away. Musicians took up its melody and stretched it into vọng cổ, the slow, moving tune at the heart of cải lương opera and of the đờn ca tài tử music that UNESCO listed in 2013. Today no wedding or gathering in the south is complete without it.

guide.price: Small entry ticket to the cape area.

hours.notes: Approximate; the national park area at the cape.

do: Wear a hat and sunscreen; boats have little shade.
Wear a life jacket on small boats.
Take a boat through the mangrove canals.
dont: Walk on the mudflats; the mud is deep.

tips.title: Local food
tips.text: Cà Mau crab, grilled fish and dried shrimp; in Bạc Liêu, try bánh xèo and local seafood.

tips.title: Getting there
tips.text: Fly or drive to Cà Mau city, then about 3 hours by road and boat to the cape.

tips.title: Nearby
tips.text: The U Minh Hạ forest, the Bạc Liêu wind farm, and the house of the Bạc Liêu prince.
